analysis.one_liner: Lets a president refuse to spend money Congress already appropriated.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 1974 Impoundment Control Act, a president who wants to hold back money Congress has appropriated must notify Congress and can only withhold it temporarily while Congress gets a chance to vote on cutting it. This bill repeals that law entirely, leaving no required procedure: a president could refuse to spend appropriated funds indefinitely, with no time limit and no congressional check. The bill was introduced by Rep. Andrew Clyde with 18 Republican cosponsors in the final weeks of the 118th Congress and never received committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: A president and the executive branch gain sweeping discretion over federal spending, because the bill removes the requirement that Congress be notified and given a chance to vote whenever the president withholds appropriated funds. An administration that wants to shrink or stall programs it dislikes — from clean-water grants to education or health funding — could simply not spend the money, without any formal rescission process or vote in Congress. Agencies and grantees that align with a president's spending priorities also benefit, since funds withheld from other programs could be redirected or banked for their use.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the only required procedure for presidential withholding: today a president must notify Congress and can withhold funds only temporarily while Congress votes on whether to cut them; repeal ends that process entirely.
Lets a president withhold appropriated funds indefinitely, since the bill strikes the Impoundment Control Act (2 U.S.C. 681 et seq.) with no replacement limits or timelines.
Removes the expedited procedures Congress can use to force votes on a president's proposed spending cuts, replacing a mandatory up-or-down mechanism with nothing.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who depend on appropriated federal spending. The Constitution gives Congress, not the president, the power of the purse; this bill would let one person effectively rewrite the budget after the fact by simply declining to spend enacted funds. Communities waiting on infrastructure, schools, health, or disaster-recovery money would have no guaranteed avenue to force its release. Congress itself also pays, in the sense that it loses the mechanism that makes its funding decisions binding.
analysis.who_pays_short: People who rely on federal programs

drawbacks.text: It removes the check that makes congressional funding decisions binding: without the act, nothing in law requires a president to spend money Congress has enacted, so a single administration could defund programs by inaction rather than through votes.

Supporters' strongest argument is that the 1974 law's rescission procedure is weak — Congress can simply ignore a president's proposed cuts — and that a president needs leverage to stop wasteful spending; the honest cost is that this bill answers that problem by removing the only process that documents withholding and forces a congressional vote, rather than strengthening it.
The bill is a single sentence of repeal with no replacement framework, so any dispute over withheld funds would fall to slow litigation, leaving grantees and program recipients with no timely remedy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated on whoever holds the presidency: maximum flexibility to redirect or shelve appropriated money. The cost falls on everyone who depends on federal programs, because it converts the budget from a law Congress passed into a suggestion a president can decline to follow. The bill offers no replacement safeguard — no notice, no deadline, no vote — so the trade is a permanent transfer of spending power from the elected legislature to one officeholder.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Budget and Rules committees without a hearing or vote until the 118th Congress ended, killing it.

narrative.text: Rep. Andrew Clyde introduced the bill on December 16, 2024, with 18 Republican cosponsors, in the last weeks of the 118th Congress.
The House referred it to the Budget Committee and the Rules Committee; neither held a markup or sent it to the floor.
No further action appears in the record before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill received no hearing and no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on appropriated federal programs, and Congress's own power of the purse, are better off because the bill never advanced: the 1974 requirement that a president notify Congress and let it vote before withholding funds stays on the books. The bill's backers gained nothing beyond a symbolic roll call of support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal program recipients and Congress's power of the purse

for.name: Rep. Andrew Clyde
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Impoundment Control Act and referred it to the Budget and Rules committees.

for.name: 18 of 226 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction, all in the final weeks of the Congress.

against.name: House Budget and Rules Committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; it received no markup or hearing before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican — 18 of 226 House Republicans joined — and no Democrat supported it; the bill was introduced too late in the Congress for any floor action either way.

industries.industry: The presidency and executive branch agencies
industries.note: Repealing the Impoundment Control Act gives a president unilateral power to withhold money Congress enacted, effectively letting the executive rewrite the budget after the fact. The cost falls on program recipients, who lose the only legal mechanism that forces withheld funds to be accounted for and voted on.
